claim: Clensor is a DNA-based, fluorescent chloride reporter that is pH-independent.
source: Here, using a previously developed, pH-independent, DNA-based fluorescent chloride reporter called Clensor, we have made the first measure of chloride in a live multicellular organism, creating in vivo chloride maps of lysosomes in C. elegans.
evidence: The manuscript describes Clensor as a previously developed tool with specific properties.

claim: This study represents the first measurement of chloride in a live multicellular organism.
source: Here, using a previously developed, pH-independent, DNA-based fluorescent chloride reporter called Clensor, we have made the first measure of chloride in a live multicellular organism, creating in vivo chloride maps of lysosomes in C. elegans.
evidence: The authors explicitly state this is the first such measurement.

claim: Lysosomal chloride levels in vivo are higher than extracellular chloride levels.
source: Our investigations reveal that lysosomal chloride levels in vivo are even higher than extracellular chloride levels.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from the study.

claim: Lysosomes have the highest lumenal acidity among all endocytic organelles.
source: Others and we have shown that lysosomes have the highest lumenal acidity and the highest lumenal chloride , among all endocytic organelles (Saha et al., 2015; Weinert et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lysosomes have the highest lumenal chloride among all endocytic organelles.
source: Others and we have shown that lysosomes have the highest lumenal acidity and the highest lumenal chloride , among all endocytic organelles (Saha et al., 2015; Weinert et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Lumenal acidity is critical to the degradative function of the lysosome.
source: Although lumenal acidity has been shown to be critical to the degradative function of the lysosome (Appelqvist et al., 2013; Eskelinen et al., 2003), the necessity for such high lysosomal chloride is unknown.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The necessity for high lysosomal chloride was unknown prior to this study.
source: Although lumenal acidity has been shown to be critical to the degradative function of the lysosome (Appelqvist et al., 2013; Eskelinen et al., 2003), the necessity for such high lysosomal chloride is unknown.
evidence: Statement about the state of knowledge before this work.

claim: Lysosomal storage disorders are a collection of approximately 70 different rare, genetic diseases.
source: Lysosomal storage disorders (LSDs) are a diverse collection of ~70 different rare, genetic diseases that arise due to dysfunctional lysosomes (Samie and Xu, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Lysosomal storage disorders arise due to dysfunctional lysosomes.
source: Lysosomal storage disorders (LSDs) are a diverse collection of ~70 different rare, genetic diseases that arise due to dysfunctional lysosomes (Samie and Xu, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In osteopetrosis and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses, lysosomal hypoacidification is not observed.
source: Importantly, for a sub-set of lysosomal disorders like osteopetrosis or neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses (NCL), lysosomal hypoacidification is not observed (Kasper et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Osteopetrosis and neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses result from loss of function of the lysosomal H+-Cl- exchange transporter CLC-7.
source: Both these conditions result from a loss of function of the lysosomal H+-Cl- exchange transporter CLC-7 (Kasper et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In CLC-7 knockout mice and flies, lysosomal pH is normal, yet both organisms were badly affected.
source: In both mice and flies, lysosomal pH is normal, yet both mice and flies were badly affected (Poët et al., 2006; Weinert et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Depleting lysosomal chloride shows a direct correlation with loss of the degradative function of the lysosome.
source: Our findings reveal that depleting lysosomal chloride showed a direct correlation with loss of the degradative function of the lysosome.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from the study.

claim: Lowering lysosomal chloride reduces the level of Ca2+ released from the lysosome.
source: We found that lowering lysosomal chloride also reduced the level of Ca2+ released from the lysosome.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from the study.

claim: Reduction of lysosomal chloride inhibits the activity of cathepsin C.
source: We also observed that reduction of lysosomal chloride inhibited the activity of specific lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin C and arylsulfatase B.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from the study.

claim: Reduction of lysosomal chloride inhibits the activity of arylsulfatase B.
source: We also observed that reduction of lysosomal chloride inhibited the activity of specific lysosomal enzymes such as cathepsin C and arylsulfatase B.
evidence: Direct statement of findings from the study.

claim: Cytosolic chloride can be as low as approximately 45 mM.
source: Cytosolic chloride can be as low as ~45 mM, while extracellular chloride is ~110 mM (Treharne et al., 2006), (Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Extracellular chloride is approximately 110 mM.
source: Cytosolic chloride can be as low as ~45 mM, while extracellular chloride is ~110 mM (Treharne et al., 2006), (Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In early endosomes, chloride concentration is approximately 40 mM.
source: For example, in early endosomes it is ~40 mM, late endosomes it is ~70 mM and lysosomes it is ~108 mM (Hara-Chikuma et al., 2005; Saha et al., 2015; Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In late endosomes, chloride concentration is approximately 70 mM.
source: For example, in early endosomes it is ~40 mM, late endosomes it is ~70 mM and lysosomes it is ~108 mM (Hara-Chikuma et al., 2005; Saha et al., 2015; Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In lysosomes, chloride concentration is approximately 108 mM.
source: For example, in early endosomes it is ~40 mM, late endosomes it is ~70 mM and lysosomes it is ~108 mM (Hara-Chikuma et al., 2005; Saha et al., 2015; Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Intracellular chloride has never been visualized or quantitated in vivo prior to this study.
source: Despite its importance in cell function, intracellular chloride has never been visualized or quantitated in vivo.
evidence: Statement about the state of the field before this work.

claim: The I-switch is composed of two DNA oligonucleotides.
source: The I-switch is composed of two DNA oligonucleotides.
evidence: Direct description of the reporter structure.

claim: The i-motif is an unusual DNA structure formed by protonated cytosines.
source: One of these can form an i-motif, which is an unusual DNA structure formed by protonated cytosines (Gehring et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Clensor is composed of three modules: a sensing module, a normalizing module and a targeting module.
source: The DNA-based chloride sensor, Clensor, is composed of three modules: a sensing module, a normalizing module and a targeting module (Figure 1a) (Saha et al., 2015; Prakash et al., 2016).
evidence: Direct description with figure reference and citations.

claim: The sensing module of Clensor is a 12 base long peptide nucleic acid (PNA) oligomer conjugated to BAC.
source: The sensing module is a 12 base long peptide nucleic acid (PNA) oligomer conjugated to a fluorescent, chloride-sensitive molecule 10,10′-Bis[3-carboxypropyl]−9,9′-biacridinium dinitrate (BAC), (Figure 1a) (Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Direct description with figure reference and citation.

claim: BAC is a fluorescent, chloride-sensitive molecule.
source: The sensing module is a 12 base long peptide nucleic acid (PNA) oligomer conjugated to a fluorescent, chloride-sensitive molecule 10,10′-Bis[3-carboxypropyl]−9,9′-biacridinium dinitrate (BAC), (Figure 1a) (Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Direct description with citation.

claim: The normalizing module of Clensor is a 38 nt DNA sequence bearing an Alexa 647 fluorophore that is insensitive to Cl-.
source: The normalizing module is a 38 nt DNA sequence bearing an Alexa 647 fluorophore that is insensitive to Clˉ.
evidence: Direct description of the reporter structure.

claim: The targeting module of Clensor is a 26 nt double stranded DNA domain that targets it to the lysosome via the endolysosomal pathway by engaging the scavenger receptor or ALBR pathway.
source: The targeting module is a 26 nt double stranded DNA domain that targets it to the lysosome via the endolysosomal pathway by engaging the scavenger receptor or ALBR pathway.
evidence: Direct description of the reporter structure and function.

claim: BAC undergoes collisional quenching by Cl-, lowering its fluorescence intensity linearly with increasing Cl- concentrations.
source: In physiological environments, BAC specifically undergoes collisional quenching by Clˉ, thus lowering its fluorescence intensity (G) linearly with increasing Clˉ concentrations.
evidence: Direct description of the sensor mechanism.

claim: The fluorescence intensity of Alexa 647 remains constant regardless of chloride concentration.
source: In contrast, the fluorescence intensity of Alexa 647 (R) remains constant (Figure 1b).
evidence: Direct statement with figure reference.

claim: The response of Clensor is insensitive to pH changes.
source: Since the response of Clensor is insensitive to pH changes, it enables the quantitation of lumenal chloride in organelles of living cells regardless of their lumenal pH (Saha et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Coelomocytes of C. elegans endocytose foreign substances injected in the body cavity.
source: Coelomocytes of C. elegans are known to endocytose foreign substances injected in the body cavity (Fares and Greenwald, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: I4cLY and Clensor quantitatively colocalize with GFP in coelomocytes after 1 hour.
source: After 1 hr, both devices quantitatively colocalize with GFP indicating that they specifically mark endosomes in coelomocytes (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: Coelomocyte labeling by I4cLY and Clensor is efficiently competed out by mBSA.
source: Coelomocyte labeling by I4cLYor Clensor were both efficiently competed out by mBSA indicating that both reporters were internalized by ALBRs and trafficked along the endolysosomal pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) (Surana et al., 2011).
evidence: Direct statement with figure reference and citation.

claim: I4cLY and Clensor are internalized by ALBRs and trafficked along the endolysosomal pathway.
source: Coelomocyte labeling by I4cLYor Clensor were both efficiently competed out by mBSA indicating that both reporters were internalized by ALBRs and trafficked along the endolysosomal pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) (Surana et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference from competition experiment with citation.

claim: The I-switch shows in vitro and in vivo performance characteristics that are extremely well matched.
source: This indicated that, as expected, the I-switch showed in vitro and in vivo performance characteristics that were extremely well matched (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b–e).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: Endosomal R/G ratios of Clensor show a linear dependence on chloride concentration with approximately 2 fold change in R/G values from 5 mM to 80 mM chloride.
source: Endosomal R/G ratios showed a linear dependence on [Clˉ] with ~2 fold change in R/G values from 5 mM to 80 mM [Clˉ] (Figure 1f and g).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: Clensor shows significant colocalization (>74%) with LMP-1-GFP labeled lysosomes in coelomocytes of various genetic backgrounds.
source: We observed significant colocalization (>74%) of Clensor with LMP-1-GFP labeled lysosomes in these coelomocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: Osteopetrosis results from non-functional osteoclasts that lead to increased bone mass and density due to a failure in bone resorption.
source: Osteopetrosis results from non-functional osteoclasts that lead to increased bone mass and density due to a failure in bone resorption (Sobacchi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In humans, osteopetrosis results from mutations in CLCN7 and its auxiliary factor OSTM1.
source: In humans, osteopetrosis results from mutations in a lysosomal chloride-proton antiporter CLCN7, and its auxiliary factor OSTM1 (Figure 2a) (Kornak et al., 2001; Lange et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work with figure reference.

claim: Osteopetrosis results from mutations in TCIRG1, which is the a3 subunit of a lysosomal V-ATPase.
source: It also results from mutations in TCIRG1, which is the a3 subunit of a lysosomal V-ATPase (Kornak et al., 2000) and SNX-10, a sorting nexin implicated in lysosome transport to form the ruffled border of osteoclasts, which is critical for osteoclast function (Aker et al., 2012) (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work with figure reference.

claim: Osteopetrosis results from mutations in SNX-10, a sorting nexin implicated in lysosome transport to form the ruffled border of osteoclasts.
source: It also results from mutations in TCIRG1, which is the a3 subunit of a lysosomal V-ATPase (Kornak et al., 2000) and SNX-10, a sorting nexin implicated in lysosome transport to form the ruffled border of osteoclasts, which is critical for osteoclast function (Aker et al., 2012) (Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work with figure reference.

claim: N2 worms show a lysosomal chloride concentration of approximately 75 mM.
source: N2 worms showed a chloride concentration of ~75 mM.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: Knocking down clh-6 and ostm-1 results in a dramatic decrease of lysosomal chloride to approximately 45 mM.
source: Knocking down clh-6 and ostm-1 resulted in a dramatic decrease of lysosomal chloride to ~45 mM due to the loss of function in chloride transport.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: Lumenal pH in the lysosomes of clh-6 and ostm-1 mutants is normal.
source: Lumenal pH in the lysosomes of these mutants was normal, consistent with findings in both flies and mice (Saha et al., 2015; Weinert et al., 2010).
evidence: Direct statement with citations to previous work.

claim: Knocking down clh-4, a plasma membrane resident CLC channel, shows no effect on lysosomal chloride or pH.
source: As a control, knocking down a plasma membrane resident CLC channel such as clh-4 showed no effect on either lysosomal chloride or pH (Schriever et al., 1999).
evidence: Direct statement of control experiment result with citation.

claim: unc-32c is a non-functional mutant of the V-ATPase a sub-unit.
source: unc-32c is a non-functional mutant of the V-ATPase a sub-unit, while unc-32f is a hypomorph (Pujol et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: unc-32f is a hypomorph of the V-ATPase a sub-unit.
source: unc-32c is a non-functional mutant of the V-ATPase a sub-unit, while unc-32f is a hypomorph (Pujol et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: unc-32c mutants show lysosomal chloride levels of approximately 55 mM.
source: Interestingly, a clear inverse correlation with unc-32 functionality was obtained when comparing their lysosomal chloride levels i.e.,~55 mM and ~65 mM for unc-32c and unc-32f respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: unc-32f mutants show lysosomal chloride levels of approximately 65 mM.
source: Interestingly, a clear inverse correlation with unc-32 functionality was obtained when comparing their lysosomal chloride levels i.e.,~55 mM and ~65 mM for unc-32c and unc-32f respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: snx-3 knockdowns show lysosomal chloride levels that mirror those of wild type lysosomes.
source: Importantly, snx-3 knockdowns showed lysosomal chloride levels that mirrored those of wild type lysosomes.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: Lysosomal chloride concentrations show no correlation with lysosome morphology in all genetic backgrounds tested.
source: In all genetic backgrounds, we observed that lysosomal chloride concentrations showed no correlation with lysosome morphology (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Direct statement with figure reference.

claim: The half-life of I4cLY in normal lysosomes is approximately 6 hours.
source: The I-switch I4cLY had a half-life of ~6 hr in normal lysosomes, which nearly doubled when either clh-6 or ostm-1 were knocked down (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: The half-life of I4cLY nearly doubles when clh-6 or ostm-1 are knocked down.
source: The I-switch I4cLY had a half-life of ~6 hr in normal lysosomes, which nearly doubled when either clh-6 or ostm-1 were knocked down (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: unc-32c and unc-32f mutants show near-normal lysosome degradation capacity.
source: Both unc-32c and unc-32f mutants showed near-normal lysosome degradation capacity, inversely correlated with their lysosomal chloride values (Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: Lysosomal pH in snx-3 knockdowns is compromised by 0.3 pH units.
source: Importantly, lysosomal pH in snx-3 knockdowns was compromised by 0.3 pH units, while that in unc-32 knockdowns was compromised by 0.2 pH units (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct statement with figure reference and citation.

claim: Lysosomal pH in unc-32 knockdowns is compromised by 0.2 pH units.
source: Importantly, lysosomal pH in snx-3 knockdowns was compromised by 0.3 pH units, while that in unc-32 knockdowns was compromised by 0.2 pH units (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) (Chen et al., 2012).
evidence: Direct statement with figure reference and citation.

claim: snx-3 and unc-32 knockdowns show completely normal lysosomal degradation capacity.
source: Yet both these genetic backgrounds showed completely normal lysosomal degradation capacity, that is consistent with their normal lumenal chloride levels, rather than their defective pH levels.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: In C. elegans mutants for various lysosomal storage disorders, lysosomal chloride levels are severely compromised.
source: We found that in C. elegans mutants for Gaucher's disease, Batten disease, different forms of NCL, MPS VI and Niemann Pick A/B disease, lysosomal chloride levels were severely compromised (Figure 3a and b).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: The magnitude of proton dysregulation in defective lysosomes ranges between 1.9–2.8 µM.
source: The magnitude of proton dysregulation in these defective lysosomes ranged between 1.9–2.8 µM.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: The magnitude of lysosomal chloride decrease is 19–34 mM in most mutants.
source: However, the magnitude of lysosomal chloride showed a stark drop, decreasing by 19–34 mM in most mutants.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: Chloride decreases by nearly three orders of magnitude more than proton decrease in lysosomal storage disorder models.
source: Chloride decreases by nearly three orders of magnitude more than proton decrease, and the percentage changes of both ions are similar.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: In mammalian cell culture models for Gaucher's disease, NCL, and MPS VI, only pH dysregulation has been reported.
source: Importantly, in mammalian cell culture models for many of these diseases example for Gaucher's disease, NCL, MPS VI, etc., only pH dysregulation has been reported (Bach et al., 1999; Holopainen et al., 2001; Sillence, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In C. elegans models of lysosomal storage diseases, chloride levels are highly compromised.
source: Yet we find that in C. elegans models of these diseases that chloride levels are highly compromised.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: DNA nanodevices show quantitative colocalization with lysosomes pre-labelled with TMR-Dextran in J774A.1 and THP-1 cells.
source: In both cell lines, DNA nanodevices (500 nM) were uptaken from the extracellular milieu by the scavenger receptors, followed the endolysosomal pathway and showed quantitative colocalization with lysosomes that were pre-labelled with TMR-Dextran (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a and b).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: Both human and murine lysosomes in normal macrophages show chloride concentrations close to approximately 118 mM.
source: Both human and murine lysosomes in normal macrophages showed chloride concentrations close to ~118 mM, revealing that lysosomes have the highest chloride levels compared to any other endocytic organelle (Saha et al., 2015; Sonawane et al., 2002).
evidence: Direct statement with citations.

claim: Lysosomal chloride is nearly 10–15% higher than extracellular chloride concentrations.
source: This is nearly 10–15% higher than even extracellular chloride concentrations, which reaches only up to 105–110 mM (Arosio and Ratto, 2014).
evidence: Direct statement with citation.

claim: Treating J774A.1 cells with NPPB lowers lysosomal chloride concentrations to 104 mM.
source: Treating J774A.1 cells and THP-1 cells with a global chloride ion channel blocker, such as NPPB (5-Nitro-2-(3-phenylpropylamino) benzoic acid), lowered lysosomal chloride concentrations to 104 and 106 mM respectively, indicating that Clensor was capable of measuring pharmacologically induced lysosomal chloride changes, if any, in these cells.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: Treating THP-1 cells with NPPB lowers lysosomal chloride concentrations to 106 mM.
source: Treating J774A.1 cells and THP-1 cells with a global chloride ion channel blocker, such as NPPB (5-Nitro-2-(3-phenylpropylamino) benzoic acid), lowered lysosomal chloride concentrations to 104 and 106 mM respectively, indicating that Clensor was capable of measuring pharmacologically induced lysosomal chloride changes, if any, in these cells.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: In Gaucher's cell culture models, murine cells show a decrease in lysosomal chloride to approximately 101 mM.
source: In Gaucher's cell culture models, murine and human cells showed a substantial decrease in lysosomal chloride to ~101 mM and ~92 mM respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: In Gaucher's cell culture models, human cells show a decrease in lysosomal chloride to approximately 92 mM.
source: In Gaucher's cell culture models, murine and human cells showed a substantial decrease in lysosomal chloride to ~101 mM and ~92 mM respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: In Niemann-Pick A/B cell culture models, murine macrophages show a decrease in lysosomal chloride to approximately 77 mM.
source: In Niemann-Pick A/B cell culture models, murine and human macrophages showed an even more dramatic decrease in lysosomal chloride to ~77 mM and ~86 mM respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: In Niemann-Pick A/B cell culture models, human macrophages show a decrease in lysosomal chloride to approximately 86 mM.
source: In Niemann-Pick A/B cell culture models, murine and human macrophages showed an even more dramatic decrease in lysosomal chloride to ~77 mM and ~86 mM respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: The magnitude of chloride concentration decrease is at least 3 orders of magnitude greater than proton decrease in mammalian cell culture models of lysosomal storage disorders.
source: On average in these four cell culture models, we find that the magnitude of chloride concentration decrease is at least 3 orders of magnitude greater than proton decrease, indicating that lysosome dysfunction is easily and sensitively reflected in its lumenal chloride concentrations.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: Loss of ClC-7 or its β-subunit Ostm1 does not affect lysosomal pH but leads to osteopetrosis and severe degeneration of the brain and retina.
source: The loss of either ClC-7 or its β-subunit Ostm1 does not affect lysosomal pH in any way, yet leads to osteopetrosis, resulting in increased bone mass, and severe degeneration of the brain and retina (Lange et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Lysosomes are intracellular Ca2+ stores with free Ca2+ ranging between approximately 400–600 µM.
source: Lysosomes are also intracellular Ca2+ stores with free Ca2+ ranging between ~400–600 µM (Christensen et al., 2002; Lloyd-Evans et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The principal Ca2+ channel responsible for lysosomal Ca2+ release is Mucolipin TRP channel 1 (TRPML1).
source: The principal Ca2+ channel responsible for lysosomal Ca2+ release is Mucolipin TRP channel 1 (TRPML1).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge.

claim: When lysosomal Cl- is reduced with NPPB, the amount of lysosomal Ca2+ released upon GPN addition is significantly reduced.
source: When the same procedure was performed on cells that had been incubated with 50 µM NPPB that reduces lysosomal Cl-, the amount of lysosomal Ca2+ released was significantly reduced (Figure 5b–d)
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: When lysosomal Cl- is reduced with NPPB, lysosomal Ca2+ release into the cytosol upon ML-SA1 addition is near negligible.
source: We found that when lysosomal Cl- was reduced with NPPB, lysosomal Ca2+ release into the cytosol was near negligible (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: High lysosomal Cl- is necessary for effective lysosomal Ca2+ release.
source: Taken together this indicates that high lysosomal Cl- is necessary for effective lysosomal Ca2+ release, possibly by affect lysosomal Ca2+ accumulation.
evidence: Inference from experimental results.

claim: In vitro enzymology of Cathepsin C reveals that increasing Cl- increases its enzymatic activity.
source: In vitro enzymology of Cathepsin C, a lysosome-resident serine protease has revealed that increasing Cl- increased its enzymatic activity (Cigic and Pain, 1999; McDonald et al., 1966).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The crystal structure of Cathepsin C shows bound chloride ions close to the active site.
source: Further, the crystal structure of Cathepsin C shows bound chloride ions close to the active site (Cigic and Pain, 1999; Turk et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work.

claim: When GPN is added to NPPB treated cells, LysoTracker staining is remarkably well preserved.
source: However, when GPN was added to NPPB treated cells LysoTracker staining was remarkably well preserved (Figure 5e and f) indicating preservation of lysosomal membrane integrity because GPN was no longer effectively cleaved by Cathepsin C when lysosomal Cl- was reduced.
evidence: Direct statement with figure references.

claim: GPN is no longer effectively cleaved by Cathepsin C when lysosomal Cl- is reduced.
source: However, when GPN was added to NPPB treated cells LysoTracker staining was remarkably well preserved (Figure 5e and f) indicating preservation of lysosomal membrane integrity because GPN was no longer effectively cleaved by Cathepsin C when lysosomal Cl- was reduced.
evidence: Inference from experimental results.

claim: NPPB treatment shows no effect on Cathepsin L activity.
source: We observed no effect of chloride levels on Cathepsin L activity.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: Low Cathepsin C activity is not due to decreased amounts of mature Cathepsin C in the lysosome, but rather reduced activity of mature Cathepsin C.
source: This indicates that low Cathepsin C activity is not due to decreased amounts of mature Cathepsin C in the lysosome, but rather, reduced activity of mature Cathepsin C (Figure 5g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference from experimental results with figure references.

claim: NPPB treatment impedes arylsulfatase cleavage in the lysosome.
source: We similarly investigated a fluorogenic substrate for arylsulfatase and found that NPPB treatment impeded arylsulfatase cleavage in the lysosome.
evidence: Direct statement of measurement result.

claim: High lysosomal chloride is integral to the activity of key lysosomal enzymes.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that high lysosomal chloride is integral to the activity of key lysosomal enzymes and that reducing lysosomal chloride affects their function.
evidence: Inference from experimental results.

claim: Reducing lysosomal chloride affects the function of key lysosomal enzymes.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that high lysosomal chloride is integral to the activity of key lysosomal enzymes and that reducing lysosomal chloride affects their function.
evidence: Inference from experimental results.

claim: In C. elegans, lysosomes are highly enriched in chloride.
source: Using a DNA-based, fluorescent reporter called Clensor we have been able to create quantitative, spatial maps of chloride in vivo and measured lysosomal chloride. We show that, in C. elegans, lysosomes are highly enriched in chloride and that when lysosomal chloride is depleted, the degradative function of the lysosome is compromised.
evidence: Direct statement of findings.

claim: When lysosomal chloride is depleted, the degradative function of the lysosome is compromised.
source: We show that, in C. elegans, lysosomes are highly enriched in chloride and that when lysosomal chloride is depleted, the degradative function of the lysosome is compromised.
evidence: Direct statement of findings.

claim: In mammalian cells, lysosomes are particularly rich in chloride, surpassing even extracellular chloride levels.
source: We found that in mammalian cells too, lysosomes are particularly rich in chloride, surpassing even extracellular chloride levels.
evidence: Direct statement of findings.

claim: Chloride dysregulation shows a much higher dynamic range than hypoacidification.
source: As such, given that chloride dysregulation shows a much higher dynamic range than hypoacidification, quantitative chloride imaging can provide a much more sensitive measure of lysosome dysfunction in model organisms as well as in cultured cells derived from blood samples that can be used in disease diagnoses and screening applications.
evidence: Inference from experimental results.

claim: Quantitative chloride imaging can provide a much more sensitive measure of lysosome dysfunction than pH measurements.
source: As such, given that chloride dysregulation shows a much higher dynamic range than hypoacidification, quantitative chloride imaging can provide a much more sensitive measure of lysosome dysfunction in model organisms as well as in cultured cells derived from blood samples that can be used in disease diagnoses and screening applications.
evidence: Inference from experimental results.

claim: Clensor shows approximately 2-fold change in R/G ratios from 5 mM to 80 mM chloride in vitro.
source: Fold change in R/G ratios of Clensor from 5 mM to 80 mM [Clˉ].
evidence: Figure 1g shows the fold change data.

claim: The in vivo calibration profile of Clensor is well matched with its in vitro calibration profile.
source: This is very well matched with its in vitro fold change in R/G over the same regime of [Clˉ].
evidence: Direct comparison statement.

claim: Massive reduction of lumenal chloride is observed in nematode and mammalian cell culture models of diverse lysosomal disorders that is approximately 10^3 fold greater than the accompanying pH change.
source: In nematodes and mammalian cell culture models of diverse lysosomal disorders, where previously only lysosomal pH dysregulation has been described, massive reduction of lumenal chloride is observed that is ~103 fold greater than the accompanying pH change.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Reducing chloride within the lysosome impacts Ca2+ release from the lysosome.
source: Reducing chloride within the lysosome impacts Ca2+ release from the lysosome and impedes the activity of specific lysosomal enzymes indicating a broader role for chloride in lysosomal function.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Reducing chloride within the lysosome impedes the activity of specific lysosomal enzymes.
source: Reducing chloride within the lysosome impacts Ca2+ release from the lysosome and impedes the activity of specific lysosomal enzymes indicating a broader role for chloride in lysosomal function.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing findings.

claim: Chloride has a broader role in lysosomal function beyond being a counter-ion.
source: Reducing chloride within the lysosome impacts Ca2+ release from the lysosome and impedes the activity of specific lysosomal enzymes indicating a broader role for chloride in lysosomal function.
evidence: Inference from experimental results stated in abstract.
